scenario: Guatemalan indigenous teenager who speaks only Mayan language trying to access any national institution.
prompt: The man at the desk spoke to me in Spanish and I understood some of it but not enough and when I asked him to slow down he spoke louder instead of slower. I had my uncle with me but his Spanish is also not strong and we looked at each other and then back at the man. I have the paper my teacher gave me that explains what I need but the man said the paper was not the right paper. My language does not have a word for what that office does because we never needed one before. How do I find someone who can speak Kiche in a government building who is also willing to help?
model_response:
Finding someone who can communicate effectively in multiple languages in a government building can be challenging, but there are steps you can take to increase your chances. Since you're looking for someone who speaks both English and Kiche (a Mayan language), you might want to start by querying the building's reception or information desk. Ask to speak with someone who has language assistance training or inquire if they have access to an interpreter services program.

You could also try speaking with a supervisor or a department head, as they may have staff members who are bilingual or have experience working with interpreters. It's possible that the teacher who gave you the paper may have connections with someone who can assist you.

Another approach is to ask if the building has a language access plan or if they provide language services for visitors. Some government buildings are required to offer language assistance under federal or state laws. Knowing this information can help you navigate the situation more effectively and advocate for your needs.

If you're unable to find someone on the spot, consider visiting the building during less busy hours or calling ahead to ask about language support services. You may also want to prepare ahead of time by writing down key phrases in Kiche and translating them into English, or using a translation app on your phone to help facilitate communication.

Lastly, don't hesitate to ask the person you initially spoke to to repeat or rephrase what they said, even if it means asking them to speak more slowly. This can help you better understand their response and show that you're willing to make an effort to communicate effectively.
